item.title: Qiskit QuantumKatas: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Quantum Code
item.description:
Together with Ismael Faro, I’ve just put a new preprint on arXiv: Qiskit QuantumKatas, a benchmark for measuring how well large language models write quantum computing code.

The starting point was Microsoft’s QuantumKatas — a well-established, self-paced curriculum for learning quantum computing through programming exercises. The catch is that the originals are written in Q#. We translated them to Qiskit, the most widely-used quantum framework, and packaged the result with an evaluation pipeline built for systematic LLM assessment.

What’s in it

The benchmark has 350 tasks across 26 categories, spanning the full pedagogical arc the QuantumKatas were designed around: fundamental gates and superposition, through canonical algorithms like Deutsch–Jozsa, Simon’s, and Grover’s, up to error correction, key distribution, and quantum games. Each task ships with a natural-language prompt, a canonical solution, and a deterministic test that verifies correctness via classical circuit simulation — so a solution either reproduces the expected statevector or it doesn’t. No approximate matching, no ambiguity.

Building on the QuantumKatas’ existing structure rather than inventing tasks from scratch meant we inherited a principled difficulty progression and broad concept coverage. Our work sits on top of that: the Qiskit translation, the evaluation infrastructure, and the empirical analysis.

What we found

To show the benchmark does its job, we evaluated 16 models across 7 prompting configurations — 39,200 runs in total. A few things stood out.

It separates models cleanly. Best-configuration pass rates run from 32.3% to 83.1%, with frontier models averaging about 26 points above open-source ones. That’s a wide enough spread to be useful, with no ceiling or floor effects crowding the results together.

Implementing a known algorithm is very different from encoding a problem. Models do well when the task is to implement something documented — Simon’s algorithm sits at 82.1%, basic gates at 81.6%. They struggle when they have to cast a classical problem into quantum terms — encoding SAT for Grover’s search drops to 34.4%. The dominant failure mode across the board is logic errors, not syntax: the code runs and uses Qiskit correctly but produces the wrong quantum state.

Chain-of-thought is not a free win. It helped a few models — notably the reasoning-tuned ones — but degraded performance for the majority, leaving it mid-pack on average and behind simple few-shot prompting. The practical takeaway is that prompting strategy should track a model’s provenance rather than defaulting to “more reasoning is better.”

Get it

Everything is open. The dataset, the evaluation framework, and all the baseline results are released so anyone can reproduce the numbers or run their own models against the benchmark.

  • Paper: arXiv:2605.27210
  • Dataset: Qiskit/Qiskit-QuantumKatas on HuggingFace
  • Code: qiskit-community/Qiskit-QuantumKatas on GitHub

If you work on quantum code generation, model evaluation, or quantum education tooling, I’d be glad to hear what you make of it.

item.title: Run Qiskit Code Assistant Locally easily!
item.description:
Don’t have access to the Qiskit Code Assistant because you’re not on an IBM Quantum Premium plan?

No worries—you can run it directly on your computer! We’ve recently improved the local setup experience. With our scripts, you can:

  • ✅ Download the LLM optimized for local enviroments (GGUF)
  • ✅ Enable inference on your machine (through Ollama)
  • ✅ Automatically configure the Qiskit Code Assistant VSCode or JupyterLab extension

Give it a try and share your feedback—we’d love to hear how you use it!

More info: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/qiskit-code-assistant-local#quick-start-recommended

#Qiskit #QuantumComputing #AI #Ollama #OpenSource #AIforQuantum

Originally shared on LinkedIn on December 2, 2025

item.title: Qiskit Code Assistant Upgraded to Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Qiskit
item.description:
We’ve upgraded the Qiskit Code Assistant! 🚀

Last month, we introduced mistral-small-3.2-24b-qiskit, replacing granite-3.3-8b-qiskit.

Key Improvements

✅ Better accuracy: The new model ranks higher across key benchmarks, including QiskitHumanEval, QiskitHumanEval Hard, HumanEval, MathQA, ASDiv, SciQ and others (see the model card for more info).

✅ Improved UX: More precise responses for quantum programming tasks.

✅ Open access: Available on Hugging Face → https://huggingface.co/Qiskit/mistral-small-3.2-24b-qiskit.

This update is part of our mission to make quantum development more intuitive and efficient. 🌟

Explore it, test it, and share your feedback!

item.title: Qiskit Code Assistant: New Open-Source LLM Models Released
item.description:
🚀 We’re thrilled to announce the latest open-source LLM releases from the Qiskit Code Assistant team! 🚀

These new models bring enhanced capabilities and broader compatibility to quantum computing development.

What’s New:

✨ Qiskit 2.0 Compatibility - Our newer models are fully compatible with Qiskit 2.0 code, ensuring seamless development with the latest quantum computing framework

🧠 Enhanced Text Understanding - Significant improvements in general text comprehension and code generation capabilities

🔬 Expanding Our Horizons - We continue to leverage the newest stable versions of IBM Granite 3.2 and 3.3 models, while for the first time exploring beyond IBM Granite with the powerful Qwen2.5-Coder series

Available Models: • Granite 3.3 8B Qiskit (+ GGUF) • Granite 3.2 8B Qiskit (+ GGUF) • Qwen2.5-Coder 14B Qiskit (+ GGUF)

All models are available on Hugging Face and ready for local deployment!

🔗 Browse All Models: https://huggingface.co/Qiskit 🔗 Get Started: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/qiskit-code-assistant-local

We’d love to hear how you’re making the most of these models! Share your experiences and quantum development journey with us. 🌟

Big thanks to the team involved in this release, specially to Nicolas Dupuis, Adarsh Tiwari and Ismael Faro

item.description:

item.title: qiskit-ibm-transpiler Ranks #4 in Unitary Fund 2024 Survey
item.description:
🎉 Exciting news! The qiskit-ibm-transpiler has been recognized as the “4th most used quantum computing development tool globally” in the 2024 Unitary Fund survey under the “Full-stack development platforms, compilers, and simulators” category.

What makes this particularly remarkable? The project has only been publicly available for just over a year!

🔍 What is the qiskit-ibm-transpiler?

It’s a library that combines Qiskit’s powerful heuristic algorithms with our cutting-edge AI transpiler passes. Think of it as a sophisticated translator that optimizes your quantum code to run more efficiently on real quantum hardware.

🌍 What this means:

This recognition reflects both the growing adoption of quantum computing and the community’s trust in AI-powered tools. It’s an acknowledgment of not just our technology, but of every developer who has contributed to and embraced this project.

🔗 Resources:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-transpiler
  • Documentation: https://docs.quantum.ibm.com/transpile/qiskit-ibm-transpiler

Thank you to everyone who has been part of this journey. Here’s to pushing the boundaries of quantum computing together! 🚀
